Why Oracle Stock Slumped Today

ORCL
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock was down by more than 8% at midday today. The slump comes on a day of weakness for AI -related stocks. In a nutshell, there are increasing concerns around the costs of AI enterprises developing frontier AI models and, in turn, their ability to pay AI infrastructure companies like Oracle.

Why Oracle is particularly exposed

The weakening sentiment is evident in the credit default swap (CDS) pricing on its debt. CDS pricing reflects thre price of insuring against a debt default. It's measured in basis points (bps), whereby 100 basis points equals 1%. So, for example, insuring $1 million in debt with a CDS at 100 bps (1%) would cost $10,000 per year.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

In the middle of 2025, the CDS on Oracle's 5-year debt stood at just 35 bps, but it closed out 2025 at 154 bps. But here's the thing. Yesterday it spiked to 360 bps, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

To put that number into context, the bond market typically assumes that 40% of a defaulted bond is actually paid out, so the implied annual hazard rate can be calculated by dividing the CDS price by the 60% loss in default. In other words, .036/0.6=.06, or 6% a year.

Over 5 years, the cumulative rate equates to almost 26%. While it's important to note this is just the bond market pricing, there is still a lot of fear in the market over Oracle. Those fears are centered on its soaring capital expenditures to fund its AI build-out, which have turned its cash flow negative.

ORCL Free Cash Flow data by YCharts

Meanwhile, Oracle's debt has soared.

ORCL Net Total Long Term Debt (Quarterly) data by YCharts

Where next for Oracle

The market is clearly worried about the sustainability of AI investment, and in such conditions it makes sense to focus on stronger players like Alphabet on weakness, rather than chase Oracle stock.

New inflation data showing the Federal Reserve's preferred metric is still running hot at 3.8% year over year -- about twice the rate it's looking for -- isn't helping matters. Investors expect borrowing costs to rise.

Capital spending jumped to $51.4 billion in the third quarter, which pushed free cash flow -- the cash left from the core business and all those investments -- to negative $9.1 billion. The company has been borrowing relatively heavily to fund the gap. I'm skeptical these bets will pay off.

Oracle Is Down 60% From Its June High. J.P. Morgan Still Sees $200 ©Bianca Constantinescu's Images from Canva
Key Takeaways

J.P. Morgan reiterated its Buy rating and $200 price target on Oracle on Nov. 23, 83% above the stock's latest close.

Oracle has paid for its AI data centers with new stock and debt, and OpenAI, which S&P says is about half its backlog, is still raising money.

The cost of insuring Oracle's debt hit a record this week, alongside CoreWeave's, so funding is still the main risk.

On fiscal 2028 earnings estimates, $200 is 18x, below Oracle's five-year average of 21x, which makes J.P. Morgan's target a reasonable one.

Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) closed at $109.51 on Nov. 24, 56% below its June 1 high. But on Nov. 23, J.P. Morgan analyst Samik Chatterjee reiterated his Buy rating and $200 price target, 83% above that close.

He's held that target since August, when it sat about 30% above the stock's $153.28.

The build-out got expensive

In the quarter that ended Aug. 31, Oracle's revenue rose 30% to $19.3 billion, but capital spending hit $28.5 billion and free cash flow was negative $5 billion. Oracle sold $20 billion of stock to help pay for it, then raised about $10 billion more in stock and $10 billion in notes on Nov. 2. S&P says OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle's backlog, while OpenAI's latest funding round has reached only half of its $30 billion target, CNBC reported.

J.P. Morgan hasn't blinked

In August, J.P. Morgan projected that Oracle's revenue would grow about 33% a year and its EPS about 29% a year through fiscal 2030. It argued that growth should earn Oracle a multiple closer to its AI infrastructure peers'. It reiterated the call the day Oracle's stock jumped on the company's statement that its OpenAI contract is fully funded. Others have pulled back: DBS cut its target to $290 from $310 on Nov. 12, keeping its Buy, and analysts' average target has fallen from $349 a year ago to $236:

Oracle (ORCL): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's still 136% above the price. Of the eight firms that weighed in this month, J.P. Morgan has the lowest target.

$200 needs about 18x

Analysts expect normalized EPS of $11.06 in fiscal 2028, which ends in May 2028, up from $10.91 three months ago:

Image from Pixabay

Today's big story: Anthropic Below Its IPO Price: Do Giants Come Back?

Oracle has a choice to make. It can keep spending to grow. Or it can take a breather and strengthen its balance sheet, the record of what it owns and owes. At Tuesday's close, Nov 24, its stock was 67% below its high. That is even after a 12% rebound on Monday. Investors are not sure which path Oracle can afford.

The story began with a sale. In September 2025, Oracle told investors it had signed $455 billion of future business. Most of it was contracts to rent out AI computing power. OpenAI was the largest customer, The Wall Street Journal reported. Oracle's stock jumped 36% in a day, to its record high. But Oracle had not built the data centers yet. So it started building, with borrowed money.

In two years, Oracle's capital spending went from $7 billion to $56 billion. The business still brings in more cash than ever. That cash is its operating cash flow. But it is not nearly enough to pay for the building. Free cash flow, the cash left after capital spending, fell to minus $24 billion. Oracle borrows the gap.

Oracle's stock is 67% below its high, and its next report is not due until December. If you would rather wait for that report before you buy, your cash does not have to sit idle. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Why Keep Building?

Almost all of Oracle's growth now comes from the new business. Its cloud infrastructure unit is home to the AI contracts. In the latest quarter, that unit accounted for more than 90% of Oracle's sales growth. Its signed future business has grown to $664 billion. Analysts expect sales of about $90 billion this fiscal year, which ends in May. If Oracle stops building, that growth stops too.

Can Oracle Take A Breather?

Yes, but it has a cost. A breather means spending no more than the business brings in. That is about $32 billion a year, instead of $56 billion. Oracle would stop adding debt. But it would deliver its contracts more slowly, and it would grow more slowly. Even that $32 billion is not fixed. Over the past year, the business brought in $47 billion. That was largely because customers started paying in advance.
